items.summary: President of India Droupadi Murmu on August 13 gave her assent to the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, which seeks to overhaul the administration and functioning of tribunals across the country and create a new National Tribunals Commission (NTC). The Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 10 without discussion amid Opposition protests. The Rajya Sabha passed it a day later. The Act seeks to make the tribunal system more independent, transparent and uniform. It also repeals the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, several provisions of which were struck down by the Supreme Court for giving excessive control to the executive over tribunals. The new law follows a series of Supreme Court judgments, including the Madras Bar Association v. Union of India cases, concerning the independence and functioning of tribunals. items.title: Why 4 in 10 Indian children go to private schools
items.summary: Four in 10 Indian schoolchildren were enrolled in private unaided schools in 2025-26, up from 35.4 percent in 2018-19, according to Unified District Information System for Education ( UDISE+ ) data. Private-school enrolment increased by about 3 million in the past year, while government schools—where 48 percent of children are enrolled—saw their numbers decline by about 2.7 million. In 12 states and two Union territories (UTs), more than half the students went to private schools. Bihar, Goa and Jharkhand had less than 20 percent enrolment in private schools, while West Bengal had under 10 percent. Parents are increasingly choosing private schools at lower levels: 71 percent students in pre-primary or kindergarten and 40 percent in primary (grades I to V) were in private schools. In contrast, about 10 percent of students at the primary level were in government schools. Research studies show, and experts say, that perceptions of learning, affordability, school performance and availability of English-medium instruction affect parents’ choices. items.title: Introducing India’s first Court Downtime Tracker

It's just one example of the countless times each week that a court website fails to load for the average litigator, litigant, journalist, or legal researcher. items.title: Independent India needs an independent press
items.summary: India’s freedom struggle was also a fight for a free press. From Tilak and Gandhi to Ambedkar and Azad, newspapers helped Indians challenge colonial power and shape political thought. items.summary: A Pune court on August 14 dismissed an intervention application filed by researcher Pankaj K Phadnis seeking permission to participate in the ongoing private criminal defamation case filed by Satyaki Savarkar (grandnephew of Vinayak Savarkar) against leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi. Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) Amol Shriram Shinde rejected Phadnis's plea, ruling that the intervenor had no legal right or locus standi to participate in the proceedings. “The intervenor who is not a family member or near relatives of late Savarkar cannot unilaterally assume unto himself the status of an aggrieved person under section 199 of Cr.P.C. to assert that his feelings were hurt and maintain the subject complaint against the accused for the alleged offence of defamation,” the Court said. The judge also imposed costs of ₹20,000 for wasting the court’s time. The judge directed Phadnis to deposit the amount with Pune District Legal Services Authority. “The intervenor has consumed more and precious time of this court. items.title: Understanding the intelligence pyramid: Why most businesses know everything and do nothing?
items.summary: In every consequential field of human endeavour, whether in the boardroom, the courtroom, or on the trading floor, one resource has consistently separated those who prevail from those who do not. The resource is intelligence: information that has been processed, placed in context, and converted into a decision within the window in which that decision still counts. Military history makes the point plainly. The intelligence failures that determined the outcomes of wars were rarely failures of collection; the signals were usually present. What failed was the architecture to convert those signals into understanding, and the discipline to act before the moment passed. Corporate history repeats the lesson, and increasingly, so does the law. When a regulator, a court, or a shareholder examines how an organisation behaved before a loss crystallised, the question is seldom whether the information existed.
